- When sentiment turns negative in the last 3–5 days, reduce forecasted price momentum; over-optimistic spikes are often followed by corrections.
- If recent history shows mean reversion (e.g., 2–3 consecutive downward moves), model should not over-forecast upward continuation.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior peak), model tends to overestimate continuation — cap forecast growth to 2–3% below peak for next 5–7 days.
- If sentiment is bullish (positive >0.5) but price history shows volatility or recent pullbacks, reduce forecast slope to avoid “sentiment-driven overreach.”
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >10% from model in first 5–7 days, adjust downward by 1–2% per day until convergence with observed trend.
- When sentiment history includes alternating +/– signals (e.g., +1, -1, +1), model should avoid averaging out trend — instead, weight recent sentiment more heavily for short-term correction.
- If model consistently overestimates 30-day price by >5% in 3+ consecutive forecasts, apply a 3–5% downward bias to next forecast, especially if sentiment is neutral or slightly negative.
